slides.heading: 5 Loops That Make Self-Improvement Self-Sustaining
bullet_points: Most improvement plateaus — not because the advice is wrong
Single-layer improvement has a structural ceiling
Recursive improvement fixes the process, not just the output
slides.speaker_note: Open on the frustration of having done the work and still plateauing — frame who this is for in the first ten seconds.

slides.heading: The Treadmill Problem
bullet_points: Read the book → start the habit → fall off → repeat
Each new habit costs the same willpower as the last
The second-order move: improve how you improve
slides.speaker_note: Name the pattern everyone has felt but hasn't seen articulated — that's the moment of recognition that earns the rest of the deck.

slides.heading: Loop 1: Fix Your Information Diet First
bullet_points: Bad inputs make every habit built on top fragile
Switch from consuming content to consuming mental models
Test: does this change what I read next — or only feel like progress?
slides.speaker_note: The distinction between updates and frameworks is the core insight — land it clearly before moving on.

slides.heading: Loop 2: Build Habit Stacks, Not Habits
bullet_points: A single habit maintains momentum — it doesn't generate it
When one behavior cues another, each link makes the next cheaper
Find the upstream keystone — usually something physical
slides.speaker_note: Concrete example: morning walk → no phone → writing first. One keystone, three behaviors. Removing it collapses the chain.

slides.heading: Loop 3: Build a Review System That Reviews Itself
bullet_points: Most journals record who you were — not who you're becoming
Once a quarter: review your reviews, find consistent blind spots
Meta-question: what am I not asking myself that I should be?
slides.speaker_note: Second-order review teaches you how you think, not just what you think — that's the distinction worth repeating here.

slides.heading: Loop 4: Find Skills That Unlock Other Skills
bullet_points: Skills exist in a network — some nodes have far more edges
Writing clearly → thinking clearly → faster learning in any domain
High-leverage skills look soft — that's why they're underinvested
slides.speaker_note: The recursive test for a skill: does getting better at this make it easier to get better at other things? If yes, it earns disproportionate investment.

slides.heading: Loop 5: Rewrite the Identity Narrative First
bullet_points: Behavior follows identity — the story you tell yourself sets your defaults
Write who you're becoming as if it's already true + one behavior as evidence
When identity updates, willpower becomes less relevant
slides.speaker_note: This is the deepest loop — make it concrete with the specific identity/behavior gap before closing on the takeaway.
